primitives.name: HierarchicalBayesianEstimation
primitives.verbatim_quote: Conclusion In this study, we have redefined seven offensive positions and three defensive positions in the NBA and employed a hierarchical Bayesian linear model to estimate positional plus-minus from 2015-16 to 2021-22 based on these offensive and defensive positions.
primitives.assumptions: The model assumes normally distributed player performance around position means, with hyperpriors on position means and variances. It uses Gibbs sampling for posterior inference.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Applicable across all seasons 2015-16 to 2021-22 without known breakdown.

reasoning_traces.think: This chapter introduces a hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate positional plus-minus (PPM) for NBA players across seven offensive and three defensive positions over eight seasons. The key insight is that traditional position labels are insufficiently granular; instead, latent player roles are extracted using k-means clustering on play-type frequency vectors. These roles serve as fixed effects in a hierarchical linear model, allowing partial pooling of estimates. The empirical findings reveal that Versatile Scorers dominate offensive PPM, while Bigs excel defensively. Notably, the variance structures differ substantially across positions, reflecting varying talent pools and strategic importance. The study also documents a narrowing gap in offensive PPM over time, driven primarily by the emergence of Roll and Cut Bigs who leverage spacing created by the three-point revolution. Limitations include treating all points equally regardless of game context and ignoring interactions between positions. Future work could incorporate game state dynamics and refine role definitions using deep learning.
